sents.text: To look inside a file, cat prints the whole thing.
For big files, head shows the first lines and tail the last ones; dash n sets how many.
And wc dash l counts the lines, which is a quick way to see how many rows a data file has.
Three keys make you fast in any terminal.
Tab completes file and folder names, so you rarely type them in full.
The up arrow brings back your last command.
And Control C stops a command that's running, or one that's taking too long.
In the lab, you'll explore Colab's sample data, build a project folder, copy a dataset into it and count its rows, all from the terminal.
Prompts and hints, never the full answer.
Linux is one tree starting at slash, and paths are absolute or relative, with dot, dot dot and tilde as shortcuts.
You move with cd, look with ls, make with mkdir and touch, copy and move with cp and mv, and read with cat, head, tail and wc.
And rm has no recycle bin, so look first.
Next time: wildcards, pipes and redirection, where the terminal gets powerful.
